## Introduction

Educational Discussions with Software Engineers, or SEED, was a project in
which I interviewed people who work in the software industry and then published
their advice on my [blog](/blog/index.qmd). The goal was to reverse the usual
educational relationship: instead of asking educators to describe the software
field, I invited the professionals who work in it every day to teach my
students and me. You can read the
[introduction to the SEED project](/blog/introducing-seed-survey/index.qmd) to
learn how the initiative started.

The SEED survey is now closed and I am no longer collecting responses. The
interviews remain some of the most useful material that I have gathered about
how software is actually built, so this page collects the lessons that the
interviewees shared with me.

## What the Engineers Taught Me

Several themes appeared in interview after interview.

- **Communication is the hardest part.** Brian Blose called requirements
  gathering "consistently the most challenging aspect in software development",
  and both Jonathan Miller Kauffman and Kara King named communication with
  business stakeholders as their greatest difficulty. Writing code is only one
  part of the job.

- **Learning never stops.** Jonathan recommended "a habit of continuous
  learning and practice", Suvarshi Bhadra observed that "the learning never
  stops", and Timothy Tsai urged engineers to look beyond the expertise that
  the current project requires.

- **Mentors and networks matter.** Brian advised identifying "someone
  knowledgeable and personable enough on your team" when no mentor is assigned.
  Kara put it plainly: "Networking is a huge advantage when searching for a
  job". Rebecca Dilla encouraged readers to reach out to people online and to
  invite an acquaintance out for coffee.

- **Look beyond the biggest employers.** Rebecca pointed out that smaller
  companies offer "a bigger chance to make an impact", Brian described a
  regional grocery chain that builds its software in house, and Timothy showed
  how a company can reinvent itself as markets change.

- **Build something from end to end.** Suvarshi recommended building "an
  application from end to end" to see how the pieces fit together, while
  Rebecca warned that, unlike a course project, the product is never finished
  and is "continually being fixed, grown, and improved".

- **Protect your time.** Suvarshi named the balance between work, personal
  hobbies, and family as the greatest challenge in the field, and Rebecca noted
  that "what you do from nine to five isn't the most important part of your
  life".
